To butter someone up means to flatter someone in an exaggerated, insincere way — with a hidden goal of getting something from them.

When you butter someone up, you compliment them, act extra sweet and kind, and make them feel wonderful about themselves — not because you genuinely mean it, but because you want a favor, a benefit, or a "yes" from them.

Think of it this way: you are coating a person with praise and sweetness, just like you spread soft, smooth butter on bread. The butter makes the bread more pleasant. Similarly, your flattery makes the person more open, warm, and willing to give you what you want.

Imagine a student who hasn't studied for an exam and needs an extension from their teacher.

Instead of just asking directly, the student walks into class and says:

"Good morning, Professor! You're such an amazing teacher. Honestly, the best I've ever had. Your explanations are so clear. I wish every teacher was like you!"

Then, a moment later: "By the way... would it be possible to get a few more days for the assignment?"

That student is buttering the teacher up. The compliments weren't coming from the heart — they were a tool to soften the teacher and make them more likely to say yes.
The Key Ingredients of This Phrase

To truly understand this phrase, remember these three core elements:

  1. The flattery is exaggerated. It goes beyond a normal, sincere compliment. It feels a little too much, a little too sweet.
  2. The flattery is strategic. There is always a motive behind it. The person buttering someone up wants something in return.
  3. It can be obvious or subtle. Sometimes people can clearly see they're being buttered up. Other times, it's done so cleverly that they don't realize it until later.
Where Does This Phrase Come From?

The most widely accepted origin traces back to an ancient Indian tradition. People would throw balls of clarified butter (called ghee) at the statues of gods and deities. The purpose was to seek favor from the gods — to please them, win their goodwill, and have their wishes granted.

This act of offering something rich and pleasing (butter) to a powerful figure in order to receive something in return mapped perfectly onto human behavior. Over time, the idea traveled into the English language as the expression "butter someone up" — meaning to lavish a person with smooth, rich praise to win their favor, just as the ancient worshippers lavished their gods with butter.

The phrase has been used in the English language since at least the early 1700s.
The Tone: Is It Positive or Negative?

This phrase carries a mildly negative or playful tone. It suggests that the person doing the flattering is being a little manipulative — not honest or straightforward. It implies:

  • The compliments are not fully genuine.
  • The person has a hidden agenda.
  • They're trying to influence or manipulate someone smoothly.

However, it is not a severely harsh phrase. In everyday conversation, people use it in a light, even humorous way — it's not an accusation of something terrible. It's more of a knowing observation: "Oh, I see what you're doing!"

Here are several examples showing how the phrase is used naturally:

  • "She spent the whole evening buttering up her dad before asking him to lend her his car."
  • "Don't try to butter me up with compliments. Just tell me what you want."
  • "He was buttering up his boss for weeks before finally asking for a raise."
  • "I know you only cleaned the kitchen to butter me up. What do you need?"
  • "Stop buttering her up — just be honest with her."

The phrase is a phrasal verb, meaning it's a verb made up of more than one word. Here is how it changes form:

  • Present: "She is buttering him up."
  • Past: "He buttered her up before the meeting."
  • Future: "I can tell he's going to try to butter the manager up."
  • Gerund (noun form): "All that buttering up won't work on me."

You can place the object (the person being flattered) between "butter" and "up" or after "up":

  • "He buttered her up." ✅
  • "He buttered up his boss." ✅

These words and phrases share a similar meaning and are useful to know alongside this one:

  • To flatter — to praise someone more than they deserve.
  • To sweet-talk — to use charming, pleasant words to persuade someone.
  • To soft-soap — to persuade someone using flattery.
  • To cajole — to gently persuade someone using kind words or false promises.
  • To suck up to someone — a more informal, slightly ruder version of the same idea.
  • To curry favor — to try to gain someone's approval through flattery or excessive helpfulness.
A Quick Way to Always Remember It

Picture this image in your mind: someone is holding a warm piece of toast, and instead of spreading butter on the bread, they are spreading it on a person — coating them in something thick, smooth, and sweet.

That's exactly what "buttering someone up" means — covering a person in a smooth layer of flattery and sweetness to make them more likely to do what you want.
To butter someone up = to shower someone with excessive, often insincere compliments or kindness, with the goal of getting a favor or benefit from them.
